How often should you release? For a long time the answer was only when we had a large batch of features to sell. In the 1990s, when our software was released on floppy disks or CD-ROMs, this made some sense. 

Release Frequency is how often working software reaches real users, and releasing more often is, in the long term, the cheaper and safer bet.

In the traditional approach to software development, we did what we called big bang releases, where we waited until the end of quarter or end of year to release our software. Basically, we would spend months working on features, doing light testing along the way. We crammed much of the real testing and other efforts into the last few weeks. This led to a lot of stress and overtime. In addition, products always went out the door with a lot of bugs. The question was not how many bugs, but how severe the bugs were.

Every release is a batch of changes. The bigger the batch, the worse each of these problems gets.

The problems with the big bang release approach are:
- Testing cost grows faster than the scope of the release, because we need to test not just for the new features, but also for their interactions.
- The more changes there are, the harder it is to find where the defects are to fix.
- The longer it has been since we last worked on a piece of code, the harder it is to understand and therefore fix a defect.
- Less feedback from the customer, on the features that we build. No matter how much User Acceptance Testing we do, it's not until the customer starts using the product in anger, that they tell us what is hard to use and what is missing.
- Customer only sees big batches so they don’t trust you to build a small version of a feature and make it better later. If they don’t demand everything and the kitchen sink in the first release, they don’t believe they will ever get it.
- Some of the features we build, will become obsolete by the time we release. For many reasons, the world around us is changing at an ever faster rate. The longer the release cycle, the more likely it is to contain features that are no longer relevant.

The most common objection is that users don’t want to deal with frequent changes. This misses a few key points:
- Not all changes need to be available all the time - limited use of Feature Flags can delay access to a feature until the audience is ready.
- When we release frequently, most of the changes are small, so it’s easier to absorb. Many of the changes are based on feedback from users and so are welcomed.
- Most people are already used to frequent changes, we use smartphones and don't notice most of the updates to the apps we use daily.

Here's a rule of thumb the agile community has spent years learning: If something hurts or is hard to do, do it more often. If it's hard to release, then release more often.

With a Scrum team that has a good Definition of Done, I would expect to increase the frequency of releases. If needed, go step by step: quarterly -> monthly -> every two weeks and eventually just move to DevOps.

## Resource Links
[Release Testing Is Risk Management Theatre (Steve Smith)](https://www.stevesmith.tech/blog/release-testing-is-risk-management-theatre/)
[Software has diseconomies of scale, not economies of scale (Allan Kelly)](https://www.allankelly.net/archives/472/software-has-diseconomies-of-scale-not/)
[Frequency Reduces Difficulty (Martin Fowler)](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/FrequencyReducesDifficulty.html)
[Using cost of delay to determine schedule (Allan Kelly)](https://www.allankelly.net/archives/432/using-cost-of-delay-to-determine/)
[The Small Batches Principle (Thomas A. Limoncelli, ACM Queue)](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2945077) - non technical explanation of why small batches are better.

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.

- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.

- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.

# Glossary Entry Creator

Create properly formatted glossary entries for the Agile Pain Relief Astro site.

## Workflow

### 1. Gather Required Information

Ask the user for:
- **Term Name**: The glossary term (can include abbreviations in brackets, e.g., "Test Driven Development [TDD]")
- **Definition/Content**: What the term means and how it's used
- **Related Terms**: Other glossary terms that relate to this one

### 2. Validate Related Terms

Before using related terms, verify they exist in the glossary. Common valid terms include:

**Core Agile:**
- `agile`, `scrum`, `kanban`, `lean`, `xp-extreme-programming`

**Roles:**
- `scrum-master`, `product-owner`, `product-owner-anti-patterns`, `scrummaster-anti-patterns`

**Events:**
- `sprint`, `sprint-planning`, `daily-scrum`, `sprint-review`, `sprint-retrospective`, `backlog-refinement`

**Artifacts:**
- `product-backlog`, `sprint-backlog`, `definition-of-done`, `definition-of-ready`, `acceptance-criteria`, `user-stories`

**Engineering Practices:**
- `agile-engineering-practices`, `test-driven-development`, `behaviour-driven-development`, `pair-programming`, `ensemble-programming`, `continuous-integration`, `continuous-deployment`, `refactoring`, `unit-testing`

**Team & Leadership:**
- `self-organization`, `team-dynamics-and-people`, `coaching`, `facilitation`, `psychological-safety`

**Anti-patterns:**
- `anti-patterns`, `scrummaster-anti-patterns`, `product-owner-anti-patterns`

**Other Common:**
- `causal-loop-diagram`, `bottlenecks`, `improvement-experiments`, `case-studies`

If unsure, check `src/content/glossary/` for the exact slug.

### 3. Generate the Slug

Create a URL-friendly slug from the term:
- Convert to lowercase
- Replace spaces with hyphens
- Remove brackets and special characters
- Keep abbreviations as part of the slug if commonly used

Examples:
- "Test Driven Development [TDD]" → `test-driven-development`
- "Sprint Retrospective" → `sprint-retrospective`
- "Definition of Done" → `definition-of-done`

### 4. Create Directory Structure

```
src/content/glossary/{slug}/
├── index.mdx
└── images/        (only if images are needed)
```

### 5. Generate the MDX File

Use this template structure:

```mdx
---
title: '{Term Name}'
date: '{YYYY-MM-DD}'
relatedTerms:
  - 'related-term-slug-1'
  - 'related-term-slug-2'
excerpt: ''
aliases:
  - 'Alternative Name'
  - 'Abbreviation'
---

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

**{Term Name}** is {definition}...

{Main content explaining the concept...}

<LinkList heading="Agile Pain Relief Blog Entries">
- [Related Post Title](/blog/post-slug/)
</LinkList>

<HighlightBox heading="Resource Links" variant="resourceLinks">
- [Resource Title](https://example.com/resource)
</HighlightBox>

<HighlightBox heading="{Term Name} Books" variant="relatedBooks">
- [Book Title](https://www.amazon.com/book-link/&tag=notesfromatoo-20) – Author Name
</HighlightBox>
```

### 6. Important Rules

**Frontmatter:**
- `title` can include abbreviations in brackets: `'Test Driven Development [TDD]'`
- `date` is the creation/update date in YYYY-MM-DD format
- `excerpt` should be left empty for the author to write (never AI-generate)
- `relatedTerms` must reference valid glossary term slugs
- `aliases` helps with search AND drives the blog auto-linker

**Aliases are required whenever the title contains a bracketed abbreviation or a suffix that readers won't type in prose.** The blog auto-linker (`src/utils/glossaryLookup.ts`) builds its match pattern from the full lowercased `title` plus every `alias`. A title like `'Test Driven Development [TDD]'` only matches that exact string (and in fact the `[...]` is interpreted as a regex character class, so the match is broken). Without aliases, neither `Test Driven Development` nor `TDD` will auto-link in blog posts.

For any title of the form `'Long Name [ABBR]'`, always add the bracket-free long form (`'Long Name'`) as an alias. Add the abbreviation alone (`'ABBR'`) only if it is 3+ letters. **Avoid two-letter aliases** — tokens like `CI`, `CD`, `UX`, `PO`, `SM` are too short: the word-boundary matcher will link them in unintended contexts (e.g., `CI` appearing inside `CI/CD`, product names, or file paths). The long form is enough.

The same applies to titles with a category suffix that readers won't always use: `'Wizard of Oz MVP'` needs `'Wizard of Oz'`, `'Fake Door MVP'` needs `'Fake Door'`, `'Agile/Lean UX'` needs `'Lean UX'`, etc. When in doubt, add an alias for any shorter form that would naturally appear in prose, subject to the two-letter rule above.

**Content:**
- Bold the term name on first use: `**Term Name**`
- Import only components actually used
- External links (`https://...`) automatically open in a new tab
- Amazon links must include `&tag=notesfromatoo-20`
- **Keep external links in the Resource Links / Related Books sections, not inline in the body.** In almost all cases a glossary entry's body prose should contain no external (`https://`) links; instead name the source in the text (e.g. "Rebecca Wirfs-Brock argues...") and put the actual link in the `resourceLinks` HighlightBox at the bottom. Internal links (`/blog/...`, `/glossary/...`) may still appear inline. Only inline an external link when the body would be incomprehensible without it, which is rare.

**Bidirectional Linking:**
- When adding `relatedTerms`, also update those terms to include this new term
- This ensures navigation works in both directions

**Sections to Include:**
1. Definition paragraph (term bolded)
2. Detailed explanation
3. Related blog posts (LinkList)
4. External resources (HighlightBox with resourceLinks variant)
5. Related books (HighlightBox with relatedBooks variant) - optional

### 7. After Creation

Remind the user to:
1. Add the `excerpt` (must be human-written)
2. Update related terms to include bidirectional links
3. Add relevant blog post links if they exist
4. Add resource links and books if applicable
5. Run `npm run dev` to preview

## Example Output

For a term "Mob Programming":

```mdx
---
title: 'Mob Programming'
date: '2025-01-25'
relatedTerms:
  - 'pair-programming'
  - 'ensemble-programming'
  - 'agile-engineering-practices'
excerpt: ''
aliases:
  - 'Mobbing'
---

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

The team gathers around a single workstation. One person acts as the "driver" who types, while the rest of the team acts as "navigators" who direct the work...

## Benefits

- Collective code ownership
- Real-time code review
- Knowledge sharing across the team
- Reduced need for meetings

<LinkList heading="Agile Pain Relief Blog Entries">
- [Why Pair Programming Works](/blog/why-pair-programming-works/)
</LinkList>

<HighlightBox heading="Resource Links" variant="resourceLinks">
- [Mob Programming - A Whole Team Approach](https://mobprogramming.org/)
- [Woody Zuill on Mob Programming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SHOVVnRB4h0)
</HighlightBox>

<HighlightBox heading="Mob Programming Books" variant="relatedBooks">
- [Mob Programming: A Whole Team Approach](https://www.amazon.com/Mob-Programming-Whole-Team-Approach/dp/B0CQXKV8NP/&tag=notesfromatoo-20) – Woody Zuill & Kevin Meadows
</HighlightBox>
```

## Handling Special Cases

### Term with Images

```mdx
---
title: 'Causal Loop Diagram'
date: '2025-01-25'
relatedTerms:
  - 'anti-patterns'
  - 'bottlenecks'
  - 'improvement-experiments'
excerpt: ''
---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import CLDExample from '@/content/glossary/causal-loop-diagram/images/cld-example.png';

A **Causal Loop Diagram** is a visual representation...

<Figure
  src={CLDExample}
  alt="Causal loop diagram showing reinforcing and balancing loops"
  caption="Example of a causal loop diagram with feedback loops"
/>
```

### Term with Multiple Sections

```mdx
**Term Name** is the primary definition...

## Overview

General explanation...

## Key Components

- **Component 1**: Description
- **Component 2**: Description
- **Component 3**: Description

## Common Mistakes

What to avoid...

```

### Term that is an Anti-Pattern

```mdx
---
title: 'Scrummerfall'
date: '2025-01-25'
relatedTerms:
  - 'anti-patterns'
  - 'scrum'
  - 'waterfall'
excerpt: ''
---

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

**Scrummerfall** is an anti-pattern where teams adopt Scrum terminology and ceremonies but continue to work in a waterfall manner...

<HighlightBox heading="Warning Signs" variant="warning">

- Heavy upfront planning for the entire project
</HighlightBox>
```

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

**Continuous Delivery** is the game of delivering features to Production whenever a change is made. It shortens the feedback and even the payment cycle, because you deliver the product more frequently. Because the steps are run multiple times a Sprint, teams need to automate all of the steps to deployment.

The application is built, and its automated test suite is run. In many organizations, it may be promoted through a staging environment where a wider suite of integration tests is performed.

In some organizations, a human (or the Product Owner 😉) decides with each build if enough additional value has been created to be worth deploying. This approach tends to be a sub-optimization.

Continuous Delivery builds on its sibling of Continuous Integration. With Continuous Integration, the team integrates their work more frequently. 

## Principles
- Build quality in
- Work in small batches
- Computers perform repetitive tasks, people solve problems
- Relentlessly pursue continuous improvement
- Everyone is responsible

Along with the benefits of feedback, continuous delivery also reduces risk since each deployment is smaller. Therefore, if there is a problem, it can be rolled back and found more easily. Some of the other business benefits: Faster time to market; Able to test product ideas sooner and reduced cost of fixing defects.

**Release Frequency** is how often working software reaches real users. Releasing more often is, in the long term, the cheaper and safer bet.

How often should you release? For a long time the answer was: only when we had a large batch of features to sell. In the 1990s, when our software was shipped on floppy disks or CD-ROMs, this made some sense.

In the traditional approach to software development, we did what we called big bang releases, where we waited until the end of the quarter or the end of the year to release our software. We would spend months working on features, doing light testing along the way, then cram much of the real testing and other efforts into the last few weeks. This led to a lot of stress and overtime. In addition, products always went out the door with a lot of bugs. The question was not how many bugs, but how severe they were.

Every release is a batch of changes. The bigger the batch, the worse each of these problems gets.

## Problems With Big Bang Releases

- Testing cost grows faster than the scope of the release, because we need to test not just the new features, but also their interactions.
- The more changes there are, the harder it is to find where the defects are so we can fix them.
- The longer it has been since we last worked on a piece of code, the harder it is to understand, and therefore fix, a defect.
- Less feedback from the customer on the features we build. No matter how much User Acceptance Testing we do, it's not until the customer starts using the product in anger that they tell us what is hard to use and what is missing.
- The customer only ever sees big batches, so they don't trust you to build a small version of a feature and make it better later. If they don't demand everything and the kitchen sink in the first release, they don't believe they will ever get it.
- Some of the features we build will be obsolete by the time we release. The world around us is changing at an ever faster rate, and the longer the release cycle, the more likely it is to contain features that are no longer relevant.

## But Users Don't Want Constant Changes?

The most common objection is that users don't want to deal with frequent changes. This misses a few key points:

- Not all changes need to be available all the time. Limited use of Feature Flags can delay access to a feature until the audience is ready.
- When we release frequently, most of the changes are small, so they're easier to absorb. Many are based on feedback from users, and so are welcomed.
- Most people are already used to frequent changes. We use smartphones and don't notice most of the updates to the apps we use daily.

## Release More Often, Not Less

Here's a rule of thumb the agile community has spent years learning: if something hurts or is hard to do, do it more often. If it's hard to release, then release more often.

With a Scrum Team that has a good Definition of Done, I would expect to increase the frequency of releases. If needed, go step by step: quarterly, to monthly, to every two weeks, and eventually just move to DevOps.

Add internal links from related blog posts and glossary entries back to a target post for improved SEO and content discoverability.

**Continuous Delivery** is the game of delivering features to Production whenever a change is made. It shortens the feedback and even the payment cycle, because you deliver the product more frequently. Because the steps are run multiple times a Sprint, teams need to automate all of the steps to deployment.

The application is built, and its automated test suite is run. In many organizations, it may be promoted through a staging environment where a wider suite of integration tests is performed.

In some organizations, a human (or the Product Owner 😉) decides with each build if enough additional value has been created to be worth deploying. This approach tends to be a sub-optimization.

Continuous Delivery builds on its sibling of Continuous Integration. With Continuous Integration, the team integrates their work more frequently. 

## Principles
- Build quality in
- Work in small batches
- Computers perform repetitive tasks, people solve problems
- Relentlessly pursue continuous improvement
- Everyone is responsible

Along with the benefits of feedback, continuous delivery also reduces risk since each deployment is smaller. Therefore, if there is a problem, it can be rolled back and found more easily. Some of the other business benefits: Faster time to market; Able to test product ideas sooner and reduced cost of fixing defects.

**DevOps** (also now DevSecOps) is the practice of Development working more closely with Operations. Over time, the Developers automate various aspects of their deployment.
